source_text: Δεικνύτωσαν δὲ, ποῦ κἂν ἔμφασις λέξεως ἀπὸ ἀλαζονείας προφερομένης παρὰ τῷ Ἰησοῦ εὑρίσκεται. πῶς γὰρ ἀλαζὼν ὁ λέγων· „μάθετε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ ὅτι πρᾷός εἰμι καὶ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ, καὶ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν“; ἢ πῶς ἀλαζὼν ὁ „δείπνου γινομένου“ ἐκδυσάμενος ἐπὶ τῶν μαθητῶν ζωσάμενος δὲ „λέντιον“ καὶ βαλὼν „ὕδωρ εἰς τὸν νιπτῆρα“ καὶ νίπτων ἑκάστου „τοὺς πόδας“ καὶ ἐπιτιμῶν τῷ μὴ θέλοντι παρέχειν αὐτοὺς καὶ λέγων· „ἐὰν μὴ νίψω σε, οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ“; ἢ πῶς ἀλαζὼν ὁ φάσκων· „κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν, οὐχ ὡς ὁ ἀνακείμενος ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ὁ διακονῶν“; ἐλεγχέτω δέ τις, τίνα ἐψεύσατο, καὶ παραστησάτω μεγάλα καὶ μικρὰ ψεύδη, ἵνα δείξῃ τὰ μεγάλα ψευσάμενον τὸν Ἰησοῦν. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλως αὐτὸν ἐλέγξαι· ὅτι ὡς οὐκ ἔστι ψεῦσμα ψεύσματος μᾶλλον ψεῦσμα. οὕτως οὐδὲ μειζόνως· ὡς οὐδὲ ἀληθὲς ἀληθοῦς μᾶλλον ἀληθὲς ἢ μειζόνως ἀληθές. τίνα δὲ καὶ τὰ ἀνόσια τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ἀπαγγελλέτω καὶ μάλιστα ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος. ἢ ἀνόσιον μὲν τὸ ἀφιστάνειν σωματικῆς περιτομῆς καὶ σωματικοῦ σαββάτου καὶ σωματικῶν ἑορτῶν καὶ σωματικῶν νουμηνιῶν καὶ καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων, μετατιθέναι δὲ τὸν νοῦν ἐπὶ νόμον θεοῦ ἄξιον καὶ ἀληθῆ καὶ πνευματικὸν μετὰ τοῦ τὸν πρεσβεύοντα „ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ“ εἰδέναι „τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις“ Ἰουδαῖον γίνεσθαι, „ἵνα Ἰουδαίους“ κερδήσῃ, καὶ „τοῖς ὑπὸ νόμον ὡς ὑπὸ νόμον,“ „ἵνα τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον“ κερδήσῃ;
pass_a_gloss: Let them show (δεικνύτωσαν) where even an appearance/hint (ἔμφασις) of a word (λέξις) brought forth from arrogance/boasting (ἀλαζονεία) is found in Jesus. For how is he a boaster (ἀλαζών) who says: 'Learn from me, for/that I am gentle (πρᾷος) and lowly (ταπεινός) in heart, and you will find rest (ἀνάπαυσις) for your souls'? Or how a boaster he who, 'supper taking place', having stripped (ἐκδυσάμενος) before the disciples, and having girded on (ζωσάμενος) a 'towel' (λέντιον), and having put 'water into the basin' (νιπτήρ), and washing each one's 'feet', and rebuking (ἐπιτιμῶν) the one not willing to offer them, and saying: 'If I do not wash you, you have no share (μέρος) with me'? Or how a boaster he who says: 'And I came to be in your midst, not as the one reclining (ἀνακείμενος) but as the one serving (διακονῶν)'? Let someone prove (ἐλεγχέτω) what he lied (ἐψεύσατο), and present great and small lies (ψεύδη), in order to show Jesus having lied the great things. It is possible also otherwise to refute him (the Jew): that as a lie (ψεῦσμα) is not more a lie than a lie, so neither more greatly (μειζόνως); as neither is a true thing (ἀληθές) more true than a true thing or more greatly true. And what are the unholy things (ἀνόσια) of Jesus, let him announce, and especially the Jew in Celsus. Or is it unholy to cause [people] to withdraw (ἀφιστάνειν) from bodily (σωματική) circumcision (περιτομή) and bodily sabbath and bodily feasts (ἑορταί) and bodily new moons (νουμηνίαι) and clean and unclean [things] (καθαρά, ἀκάθαρτα), and to transfer (μετατιθέναι) the mind (νοῦς) onto a law worthy of God (θεοῦ ἄξιος) and true and spiritual (πνευματικός), along with the one acting as ambassador (πρεσβεύοντα) 'for Christ' knowing (εἰδέναι) to become a Jew 'to the Jews' 'that he may gain (κερδήσῃ) Jews', and 'to those under law as under law', 'that he may gain those under law'?
pass_b_english: Let them show where in Jesus there is found even a hint of a word spoken out of arrogance. For how is he arrogant who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29)? Or how is he arrogant who, “during supper” (John 13:2), took off his garment in the presence of his disciples, tied a “towel” around himself, poured “water into the basin” (John 13:4–5), washed the “feet” of each one, rebuked the one who was unwilling to offer his, and said: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me” (John 13:8)? Or how is he arrogant who says: “And I was among you, not as the one who reclines at table, but as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27)?

Let someone prove what lies he told, and set out which lies are great and which small, so as to show that Jesus told the great ones. There is also another way to refute the Jew: just as no lie is more of a lie than another, so neither is one lie greater than another; just as no truth is more true than another, or more greatly true.

And let Celsus’s Jew, above all, declare what Jesus’ unholy deeds were. Or is it unholy to draw people away from bodily circumcision, a bodily sabbath, bodily feasts, bodily new moons, and clean and unclean things, and to turn the mind toward a law that is worthy of God, true and spiritual (Romans 7:14), while the one who is an ambassador “for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20) knows how to become a Jew “to the Jews, that he may win Jews”, and “to those under the law as under the law, that he may win those under the law” (1 Corinthians 9:20)?

choices.why: Luke 22:27: 'I too have been among you' -> 'And I was among you' (κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην; 'too' was a wrong sense of καί).
Lie/truth sentence reworded so the contrast μᾶλλον / μειζόνως reads plainly ('more of a lie' / 'greater'; 'more true' / 'more greatly true').
Matthew 11:29, John 13:2-8, Luke 22:27, Romans 7:14, 2 Corinthians 5:20, 1 Corinthians 9:20 checked against the verses.

translator_notes: Origen answers Celsus’s Jew, who had charged (just before this chapter) that Jesus was boastful, told great lies and did unholy things; ‘the great ones’ echoes the Jew’s phrase τὰ μεγάλα ψευσάμενον, kept unquoted because Origen reports it indirectly. Matthew 11:29: ὅτι rendered ‘for’, as in the Gospel. John 13:2-8 is cited by phrases (δείπνου γινομένου, λέντιον, ὕδωρ εἰς τὸν νιπτῆρα, τοὺς πόδας, ἐὰν μὴ νίψω σε...); ἐκδυσάμενος is Origen’s paraphrase of τίθησιν τὰ ἱμάτια (13:4). Luke 22:27 is paraphrased (Gospel: ἐγὼ δὲ ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν εἰμι ὡς ὁ διακονῶν, after ‘who is greater, the one who reclines or the one who serves?’). ‘Spiritual law’ is a clear allusion to Romans 7:14 (ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν). The list sabbath, feasts, new moons, clean and unclean may also echo Colossians 2:16; left uncited inline as uncertain. καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων has no noun; rendered ‘clean and unclean things’ (food laws are meant). ‘To refute him’ (αὐτὸν ἐλέγξαι): the person refuted is the Jew, made explicit in Pass B. Luke 22:27: κἀγὼ ἐγενόμην is ‘and I was’, not ‘I too’. The lie/truth sentence keeps Origen’s pair μᾶλλον (‘more’) and μειζόνως (‘greater, more greatly’).
